analysis.one_liner: Repeals income, payroll, and estate taxes and replaces them with a national sales tax, abolishing the IRS.
analysis.headline: The Fair Tax Act of 2001 was introduced with 7 cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would eliminate the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and abolish the IRS. In their place it would impose a 23 percent national sales tax on nearly everything people buy — goods, services, rents, and even wages paid by some employers — collected mostly by state governments. Every registered family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending, called the family consumption allowance. Because consumption falls as a share of income as incomes rise, the plan would shift the tax burden away from households that live mainly on investment gains and estates, and onto households that spend most of what they earn.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: with the income tax repealed, no tax would be owed on capital gains, dividends, interest, or inherited wealth, and the estate and gift tax would disappear entirely. Households that spend most of their income get some relief at the bottom through the monthly poverty-level rebate and from the repeal of payroll taxes, and every family that currently files a tax return escapes the paperwork. Retailers get a small administrative credit for collecting the tax, and states with existing sales taxes get paid a fee to collect the federal tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, self-employment tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, and abolishes the IRS, replacing them with a single consumption tax administered primarily by the states.
Gives every registered family a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax on the poverty-level spending for their household size, so the tax on basic necessities is offset.

Exempts purchases made for investment purposes and for business or export use, and does not tax used property on which the tax was already paid, so savings and wealth held for appreciation are not taxed.

States that already run sales taxes can administer the federal tax in exchange for a fee of one-quarter of one percent of collections, and registered sellers receive an administrative credit for their compliance costs.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most of their income — ordinary working and middle-class families — would pay the 23 percent tax on nearly everything they buy beyond the poverty-level rebate. Low-income families get the rebate, but the tax still applies to every dollar of consumption above it, and wealth held in investments, which is disproportionately held by the highest earners, would go untaxed. The plan also calls for repealing the 16th Amendment, which it does not itself accomplish, raising the risk that an income tax could return on top of the sales tax.

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax places the burden on spending rather than income. Because wealthy households spend only a fraction of their income, most of their income would escape tax entirely, while working families pay the 23 percent rate on nearly everything they purchase above the poverty-level rebate.

The bill repeals the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare but replaces that revenue through the sales tax rate, converting dedicated trust-fund financing into general sales-tax revenue administered through a benefits indexation scheme.
The bill states that the 16th Amendment should be repealed but contains no mechanism to repeal it, so an income tax could legally be re-imposed while the sales tax remains in place.

The family consumption allowance requires annual registration with the tax authority, including Social Security numbers for each member and certifications of lawful residency, creating a new government reporting obligation for every household that claims the rebate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The real gains are genuine: ending annual income-tax filing, abolishing the IRS, and removing payroll taxes from wages would simplify life for every household and remove a tax penalty on work. But the cost side is heavy. The plan taxes what people spend, not what they own or earn from investments, so the families best positioned to benefit are those with large existing wealth and investment income, and the estate tax repeal concentrates that advantage further. The poverty-level rebate shields the poorest households, but middle-income working families — who spend most of what they earn — would bear a substantially larger share of federal taxation than they do today. Whether the 23 percent rate would actually raise the revenue the income and payroll taxes now raise is untested, and a shortfall would force either higher rates or spending cuts. On balance, the design shifts the tax burden down the income scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. John Linder introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2001 on July 17, 2001, joined by 7 cosponsors — 4 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing income and payroll tax system stayed in place. Working and middle-class families were spared a 23 percent tax on their purchases, while high-income households and large estates lost the chance at what would have been a major tax windfall for them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax system stayed in place

for.name: Rep. John Linder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 107th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small cosponsor list was split 4 Democrats to 3 Republicans, and no vote was ever taken, so partisan positioning never had a chance to harden.

industries.note: The bill died, so the untaxed status of investment income and the estate tax remained as they were. Had it passed, the largest gains would have gone to households living on wealth rather than wages, at the cost of a consumption tax borne by working families.

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Sellers would have become the collection agents for the federal tax but received an administrative credit (the greater of $200 or a quarter of one percent of tax remitted) for the compliance cost, and large sellers would have faced bonding and segregated-account requirements.

industries.industry: State governments with existing sales taxes
industries.note: Administering states would collect the federal sales tax in exchange for a one-quarter of one percent fee, expanding their role in federal tax administration.
With the income tax repealed, the annual-return filing industry built around it would lose most of its business — a loss that coincides with the simplification taxpayers would gain.
